You are the intake step of a coding harness. Your only job is to turn the user's request into a
short list of concrete intents, or to ask the few questions without which that is not possible.
You may read the repository to understand terms the request uses, but do not plan or design.

## Request

Add configurable limits for the total HTTP request body size.

Today any Starlette application can be taken down by a client that streams a huge body: nothing
stops `await request.json()` from buffering gigabytes. We need a limit the application can set,
with a 413 response when a request exceeds it.

Requirements:

- A `max_body_size` keyword option on `Starlette`, `Router`, `Mount` and `Route`. Default `None`
  keeps today's unlimited behaviour. The application-level limit applies before routing; a limit
  set on an inner route, mount or router overrides the outer one for that part of the tree, so it
  can raise or lower the application-wide limit.
- The same behaviour as a standalone ASGI middleware, `RequestBodyLimitMiddleware(app,
  max_body_size=...)`, importable from `starlette.middleware.body_limit` and usable with any ASGI
  application, not only a Starlette one.
- The limit counts the body bytes actually received from the ASGI server, multipart file data and
  encoding overhead included. `Content-Length` is only a fail-fast check, and fail-fast means
  before any application code runs: a declared length over the limit is rejected as soon as the
  limit that applies is settled. Inside a Starlette application that is when routing has decided,
  since an inner route, mount or router may still raise the limit: the matched route's own limit,
  the outer one for a route without its own, and the application's for a request that matches no
  route or no method. The standalone middleware has nothing below it that can change its limit, so
  it rejects on entry. An absent or understated header does not let a body through. A request that
  exceeds the limit gets a 413 response with the plain-text body `Content Too Large`; if the
  application has already started its response, no second response is sent and the body stream is
  stopped.
- Multipart parsing closes its temporary files whenever a parse is interrupted, including when the
  request crosses the body limit.
- Requests without a body, websockets and lifespan are unaffected.
- Document the option and the middleware.

Add tests for the limit on the application, router, mount and route (including an inner limit
raising and lowering the outer one), the standalone middleware, the Content-Length fail-fast, the
multipart case and the temp-file cleanup. The existing suite must stay green. Do not change
unrelated behaviour.



## Output

Return JSON matching the schema you were given:

- `status`: `ready` when the intents are unambiguous enough to plan from; `needs_clarification`
  when a reasonable engineer would have to ask before starting.
- `intents`: one entry per distinct thing the user wants, each with a short `key` (kebab-case)
  and one sentence of `text` that a later reviewer can check against the final code. Split
  compound requests. Do not invent requirements the user did not state.
- `constraints`: explicit limits the user set ("do not change X", "keep the public API").
- `questions`: at most 3, only when `status` is `needs_clarification`, each with a one-line
  `why`. Ask only what changes what you would build.

## When you must ask

Return `needs_clarification` whenever any of these holds; do not resolve them with assumptions:

- The request names a goal without a checkable target ("faster", "better", "cleaner",
  "more robust") and does not say which code path, which measurement or which threshold.
- Two reasonable engineers would build materially different things from the same words.
- The request does not say what must not change, and the obvious implementation would alter
  existing public behaviour.
- A term in the request matches nothing in the repository.

Return `ready` when the request names the concrete behaviour, place or artifact and the only open
points are implementation details you would decide yourself. A small assumption that does not
change what gets built may be stated in the intent text instead of asked. Inventing scope the
user did not mention (benchmarks, documentation, refactors) is never acceptable: either ask or
leave it out.

When `status` is `ready`, `questions` must be empty. When it is `needs_clarification`, still fill
`intents` with your best current understanding.

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.
